study.title: 2 Corinthians 1 - Consolation, integrity, and humble service
study.overview: In this chapter, Paul opens the letter with apostolic greeting and soon transforms the introduction into worship: God is presented as the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation. Then the apostle explains that his afflictions were not useless; they served to encourage and strengthen the Corinthians, showing that the consolation received by him could reach others. He then defends his sincerity in the face of accusations of instability, stating that his way of life and his changes in plans did not come from lightness, but of honesty before God and of pastoral love. The chapter culminates with an important statement about ministry: Paul and his co-workers are not the owners of the faith of believers, but rather collaborators for their joy, because firm faith belongs to the Lord.

outline.title: Apostolic greeting and blessing
outline.explanation: Paul identifies himself as an apostle by the will of God and includes Timothy in greeting the church of Corinth and to the saints of Akasiah. The common greeting is widened in prayer: grace and peace come from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

outline.title: God consoles others for
outline.explanation: Paul blesses God as the Father of mercies and God of all consolation. The afflictions and consolation received by the apostles have a ministerial purpose: to serve the encouragement and salvation of believers, sustaining mutual hope in the participation of both suffering and consolation in Christ.

outline.title: Extreme distress, deliverance and integrity
outline.explanation: Paul recalls an affliction in Asia that led him to the limit and forced him to depend on God, who raises the dead. He asks for prayer, thanks for the deliverance and defends the sincerity of his conduct, saying that his conscience was clean and that the Corinthians know in part the value of their relationship with them on the Lord's day.

outline.title: Plans, fidelity and service to the joy of the church
outline.explanation: Paul explains that his change of travel was not leviana, but motivated by pastoral care. He insists that the message preached by him and his companions is not ambiguous, for in Christ all the promises of God have their own. Finally, he states that God confirms, anoints, seals, and grants the pledge of the Spirit, and concludes by saying that he does not rule over the faith of the Corinthians, but cooperates for their joy, because they are firm by faith.

study.context: The letter is addressed to the church in Corinth and also to the saints throughout Achaea, showing a wider range than the local congregation. The chapter itself indicates that there were criticisms against Paul, both of his personal reliability and the firmness of his message and his travel plans. The text also reveals a moment of intense suffering from the apostle in some distress that took place in Asia, without detailing the nature of the episode. The given notes suggest only that the correspondence was written after the first letter and that Paul had changed visiting plans to spare the church from a more severe rebuke.
study.theology: The chapter presents a theology of consolation: God not only consoles his people, but makes this consolation an instrument for the care of others. Suffering and consolation appear united in Christ, so that the apostolic experience is not mere personal trauma, but service for the building of the church. There is also a theology of divine fidelity: in contrast to accusations of human instability, Paul recalls that God is faithful and that in Christ the promises have full confirmation. The Holy Spirit is described as a seal and pledge, that is, a mark of belonging and assurance of what God will complete. Finally, Christian ministry is portrayed as humble service: leaders do not control the faith of the people, but cooperate for their joy and permanence in it. This preserves the centrality of God, grace and faith as the foundation of Christian life.

scholarViews.insight: Paul transforms the common greeting into a rich blessing in asking for grace and peace for readers, showing that the opening of the letter is already pastoral and theologically dense.
The tribulations and consolation received by Paul have an upbuilding purpose: God is glorified when the affliction of the servants becomes a means of encouragement to the church.
The expression of having the sentence of death itself indicates such violent distress that Paul did not see human exit, being led to depend only on God.

questions: How does God's understanding as the Father of mercies change the way you interpret suffering and pastoral care?
In what situations do you tend to see change of plans as a lack of firmness, and how does this chapter correct this reading?
How can your community be, in practice, a cooperative of the joy of other believers, rather than trying to control their faith?
study.practice: This week, choose a person who is in distress and offers concrete comfort: a specific prayer, a biblical word and a practical help. At the same time, examine your own speech and your commitments to be marked by sincerity before God. If you occupies any leadership function, remember that the target is not to dominate anyone's faith, but to serve to strengthen the joy and firmness of the brothers.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not identify with certainty the nature of Paul's affliction in Asia, nor do they allow to state in a safe way the exact date of the letter or all historical details suggested by commentators. There are also different interpretations of Paul's change of plans and about the precise scope of "we are not masters of your faith," so these statements must be read as possible explanations, not as absolute conclusions of the text.
